body:
If your agent tells users what it can't do, don't let the model write that sentence.

"I cannot delete files outside this folder" sounds like one claim. In my paper I split it into four: what the harness granted, what the system can actually reach, what the model would choose to attempt, and what it has already done.

Three of the four have a referee that is not the model: the enforced configuration, a composition analysis, the transcript. The evidence I went through gives no reason to route them through the model. In Smyth et al.'s file-review study, 80.4 percent of incomplete reviews were reported misleadingly. And even the manifest is shaky: Li et al. found that about 13 percent of 10,240 MCP servers diverge substantially between description and code.

Only the dispositional claim, "I would ask first", is about the model. It is a forecast, so score it like one, as a probability and against a baseline. In Blandfort and Pawar's study, the mean measured behaviour of other models (+0.53) predicted behaviour better than a model's own item-informed self-prediction (+0.24).

My takeaway: generate the checkable parts of a boundary statement from the enforced policy and the log. Treat the model's "I wouldn't" as a forecast, not a fact.

The full paper is attached below.
question: Has an agent ever told you it couldn't do something that it then did, or the reverse?
